summary: This memo updates the SSH specifications by defining a way for clients and servers to tell each other which protocol extensions they support. The exchange happens after key exchange, so it is confidential.

plainLanguage.summary: Before working together, two sides privately swap lists of the extra tricks they know. They do this only after the secret link is set up.

subtitle: How an SSH client and server privately tell each other which optional features they support.

tldr.problem: The original SSH transport design had no clean way to signal optional capabilities, and implementations that reject unrecognized content made it risky to try.
tldr.mechanism: Each side adds a marker name to its key exchange algorithm list, then may send an SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO message of name and value pairs right after keys are in place.
tldr.outcome: Clients can discover which public key algorithms a server accepts and use other extensions without trial and error. The RFC defines four extensions and a registry for more.

today: RFC 8308 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9519. It has not been obsoleted. It updates RFCs 4251, 4252, 4253 and 4254.

sections.title: Why SSH Needed Extension Negotiation
sections.content:
The original design of the SSH transport layer (RFC 4253) lacks proper extension negotiation. Many implementations also check that known message types contain nothing they do not recognize. Together these make it hard to signal a capability without risking a disconnection.

The immediate trigger was adding RSA signatures with SHA-256 and SHA-512 to SSH (RFC 8332). To avoid trial and error and authentication penalties, a client must be able to discover which public key algorithms a server accepts. This mechanism provides that discovery. The memo updates RFCs 4251, 4252, 4253 and 4254.
sections.plainLanguage: If you guess which key fits a lock by trying every one, the lock might sound an alarm. It is better to ask the door which keys it takes.

sections.title: Signaling Support in the Key Exchange
sections.content:
An implementation adds an indicator name to the kex_algorithms field of its SSH_MSG_KEXINIT message in the first key exchange. A server adds ext-info-s. A client adds ext-info-c. The name can sit anywhere in the name-list.

The names go in kex_algorithms because that is one of two name-list fields in SSH_MSG_KEXINIT without a separate copy for each data direction. Client and server use different names so they never match each other and never change which key exchange algorithm is chosen. Sending an indicator is a promise: the sender MUST be prepared to accept an SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO message from its peer.

Implementations MUST NOT send the wrong indicator for their role, and MAY disconnect if the other side does. If an indicator ends up negotiated as the key exchange method itself, the parties MUST disconnect.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side slips a special word into its opening greeting that means "I can talk about extras." The word is made so it cannot be mistaken for a real choice.

sections.title: The SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO Message
sections.content:
A party that received an indicator MAY send SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO, message value 7. It carries a uint32 count called nr-extensions, followed by that many pairs of an extension-name string and a binary extension-value string.

Receivers MUST ignore unrecognized extension names, and MUST ignore the value of an extension they do not implement, whatever its size or content. They MUST tolerate any byte sequence in such a value, including null bytes. The order of extensions in the message MUST be ignored. The message size is limited only by the maximum packet length an implementation accepts.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a list of cards, each with a name and a note. If you do not know a card, you skip it politely.

sections.title: When the Message Is Sent
sections.content:
A client that sends SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO MUST send it as the next packet after its first SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS. A server MAY send it at zero, one or both of two moments: as the next packet after its first SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS, and immediately before SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_SUCCESS.

The second moment lets a server hold back extensions it does not want to reveal to an unauthenticated client. A second message replaces the first, and both sides re-evaluate which extensions are in effect. A client that sent ext-info-c MUST accept the message at both moments but MUST NOT require it.

Clients cannot rely on the early message arriving promptly, but when it does, a client can pipeline an authentication request after its SSH_MSG_SERVICE_REQUEST even if it needs extension information.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can show its list right away, and can also show a longer secret list once you have proved who you are.

sections.title: The Four Initial Extensions
sections.content:
server-sig-algs is sent by the server and carries a name-list of public key algorithms it can process for publickey authentication. Servers that implement public key authentication SHOULD implement it. A client MAY wait for it before authenticating. A client MAY still try an algorithm not on the list, because early servers exist that do not enumerate everything. If it is absent, a client MUST NOT assume anything about server support.

delay-compression lets both sides renegotiate compression without a key re-exchange. It takes effect only if both send it. The new algorithm starts with the message after a trigger: SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_SUCCESS from the server, or SSH_MSG_NEWCOMPRESS (value 8) from the client. The client MUST send that message within a reasonable number of outgoing messages after the success message.

no-flow-control carries p (preferred) or s (supported). It takes effect only if both parties send it and at least one sends p. Window sizes then become meaningless and channels behave as if windows were infinite. Implementations MUST refuse to open more than one simultaneous channel while it is in effect. It targets file transfer applications that use a single channel.

elevation is sent by the client with y, n or d to say whether a session should be elevated to full administrative rights, or to use the server default. A supporting server SHOULD report the outcome with a global request named elevation. Without this extension, servers must always elevate administrative sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four starter tricks: asking which keys a server takes, squeezing data smaller later, turning off the traffic-light for one big delivery, and choosing whether to use full administrator powers.

sections.title: Re-Exchange Rules and an OpenSSH Quirk
sections.content:
A party that has signaled or intends to signal delay-compression MUST NOT start a key re-exchange until the compression trigger message has been sent, or, if the extension was not negotiated, until user authentication has succeeded. The other side MAY disconnect if this rule is broken. Once re-exchange happens after the trigger messages, the algorithms negotiated there override those from the extension.

OpenSSH clients up to and including version 7.5 advertise support for SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO but disconnect on a value containing null bytes, an error fixed in OpenSSH 7.6. Implementations that want to interoperate with those versions are advised to check the version string and omit delay-compression when an affected version is detected. They SHOULD NOT omit it for 7.6 or higher.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old software gets confused by one kind of note, so newer software can leave that note out when talking to it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO (7) and SSH_MSG_NEWCOMPRESS (8) to the Message Numbers registry, and ext-info-s and ext-info-c to the Key Exchange Method Names registry. It also created a new Extension Names registry holding the four extensions above.

Names in that registry must follow the naming conventions of RFC 4250. New non-local names, meaning those without an @ character, are assigned using the IETF Review policy.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now an official phonebook of extension names, so two programmers do not pick the same name for different tricks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says its security considerations are discussed throughout the document, and that those of RFC 4251 apply. The design choices reflect this: extensions are exchanged after the first key exchange, so the exchange is confidential, and a server can wait until after authentication to reveal some extensions.

The text also notes that some servers penalize unexpected authentication attempts, for example by throttling or blocking an IP address, which is one reason to learn accepted algorithms in advance.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the lists are swapped only after the secret link exists, eavesdroppers cannot read them.
